Three categories of bug: syntax errors, runtime errors (exceptions), and logic (semantic) errors
A systematic method: reproduce, isolate/localize, form a hypothesis, test it, fix, verify no regression
Common tools and techniques: print/logging, a debugger with breakpoints and stepping, reading stack traces, rubber-duck debugging
A concrete worked example of finding a logic bug

claims.claim: Programming defects fall into three broad kinds: syntax errors caught before the program runs, runtime errors (exceptions) raised during execution, and logic/semantic errors where the program runs but produces the wrong result.
A syntax error is detected by the parser before execution; the code is not valid Python and the program does not run at all until it is fixed.

Even syntactically correct code can raise an error during execution; such errors are called exceptions, and their type is printed with the message (for example ZeroDivisionError, NameError, TypeError).
A semantic (logic) error is a problem with a program that runs without producing an error message but does not do the right thing.

A debugger such as Python's pdb supports setting breakpoints, single stepping at the source line level, inspecting stack frames, listing source, and evaluating expressions in the context of a stack frame.

The words 'bug' and 'debugging' predate the 1947 Harvard Mark II moth taped into the operations log with the note 'first actual case of bug being found'; 'bug' for a technical fault goes back to the 1800s (Edison), and Grace Hopper popularized the moth story though the log entry was not recorded by her.

A reliable debugging method moves in steps: reproduce the failure, isolate/localize it to a small region, form a hypothesis about the cause, test the hypothesis, apply a fix, then verify the fix works and did not introduce a regression.

A function intended to return the largest element of a list but initialized with a running maximum of 0 returns 0 for an all-negative list such as [-5, -2, -9], which is a logic error visible only on certain inputs; seeding the running maximum with the first element fixes it.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Who found and recorded the 1947 moth, and whether it is the 'first' computer bug.
positions: Popular retellings credit Grace Hopper with finding the moth and coining 'bug'.
The Computer History Museum notes a team member recorded the log entry and that Hopper made the incident famous later; the term 'bug' already existed, tracing to Edison in the 1800s.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Present the anecdote as the origin of the preserved log entry and a memorable story Hopper popularized, explicitly stating the term predates 1947 and that Hopper did not herself record the note.
